summary: This informational document discusses the security implications of generating IPv6 atomic fragments and several interoperability issues they cause. It concludes that generating them is undesirable and documents the motivation for removing the functionality in a future revision of the specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a computer wraps a small package in a special sticker meant for split packages. That causes trouble and security risks, so this says to stop doing it.

subtitle: Why sending IPv6 packets with fragment headers is a security risk.

tldr.problem: IPv6 allows hosts to add a fragment header to packets that are not actually fragmented, creating security vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents how forged error messages can trick hosts into adding these headers, enabling denial-of-service attacks against networks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends removing this feature from IPv6. IPv4/IPv6 translators should not send error messages that trigger it, and hosts should ignore such messages.

today: RFC 8021 is an Informational document. It recommends deprecating IPv6 atomic fragments. This recommendation has been incorporated into RFC 7915 and other IPv6 standards, so the feature is being phased out of modern implementations.

sections.title: The IPv6 Atomic Fragment Problem
sections.content:
The IPv6 fragmentation specification allows hosts to add a Fragment Header to any packet, even when the packet is not actually fragmented into pieces. The RFC calls these "atomic fragments".

They were created to solve a problem with IPv4/IPv6 translation: when a translator sends an error message with a very small MTU (maximum packet size), IPv6 hosts must add this header to tell translators how to set the IPv4 Identification field. However, atomic fragments create more problems than they solve and should be deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: Some packets get a shipping label meant for broken packages, even though they are not broken. This was meant to help translators, but it causes trouble instead.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
An attacker can forge an error message claiming the path MTU is too small. This tricks a host into adding Fragment Headers to all its packets. If intermediate routers drop packets with extension headers (which many do to prevent attacks), the host's traffic gets silently discarded.

This attack is powerful because the attacker does not need to spoof the source address of the error message itself, only the addresses inside the error's payload. Additionally, many implementations do not validate these error messages properly. A single forged message can affect multiple connections to a destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor can send a fake message telling a computer that a road is too small. The computer then adds the broken-package label to everything it sends. But networks see that label and throw the packages away, breaking all communications.

sections.title: Technical Limitations
sections.content:
Atomic fragments depend on several unreliable mechanisms: error messages must reach the destination (but many networks drop them), hosts must respond to these messages (but 57% of tested servers do not), and the fragment header information must be accessible to translators (but some operating systems hide it).

The RFC notes that SIIT (Stateless IP/ICMP Translation), the only protocol relying on atomic fragments, has already been superseded by RFC 7915, which does not use them. The gain of atomic fragments is minimal compared to their risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Atomic fragments rely on messages that often get lost, servers that do not respond, and technical information that is hard to access. The one system that needed them found a better way.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends two changes: IPv4/IPv6 translators should no longer send error messages with MTU values smaller than the IPv6 minimum of 1280 bytes, and IPv6 hosts should ignore such messages as invalid. These changes ensure that there is no legitimate reason for hosts to generate atomic fragments.

These recommendations have been incorporated into updated IPv6 specifications including RFC 7915, the current IPv6-to-IPv4 translation standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Stop sending fake "too small" messages, and stop believing them when you hear them. Then no computer will ever need to use the broken-package label.
